items.followUp: Name the four major types of biomolecules and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks two correct biomolecule type-example pairs.
rubric.description: Names carbohydrates and proteins and gives one correct example of each.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both correct type-example pairs.

rubric.why: Checks the remaining two correct biomolecule type-example pairs.
rubric.description: Names lipids and nucleic acids and gives one correct example of each.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both correct type-example pairs.

modelAnswer: The four major types of biomolecules are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
Examples: glucose is a carbohydrate, an enzyme is a protein, fat is a lipid, and DNA is a nucleic acid.

items.followUp: How did Ronald Ross show that mosquitoes transmit malaria?

rubric.why: Checks King's observation linking malaria to places where mosquitoes were abundant.
rubric.description: States that malaria was common in marshy or swampy places where mosquitoes were plentiful.

rubric.why: Checks King's proposal that mosquitoes were involved in spreading malaria.
rubric.description: States that King proposed mosquitoes could spread or carry malaria.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the proposed link between mosquitoes and malaria.

modelAnswer: A.F.A. King observed that malaria was common in marshy places where mosquitoes were plentiful.
He also noted that people sleeping outdoors were more likely to get malaria, and proposed that mosquitoes could spread the disease.

items.followUp: Why are viruses not placed in any of the five kingdoms?

rubric.why: Checks the non-cellular nature of viruses.
rubric.description: States that viruses are acellular or lack cellular structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying viruses as acellular.

rubric.why: Checks the distinctive living and non-living status of viruses.
rubric.description: States that viruses show both living and nonliving characteristics and are not placed in any of the five kingdoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating their borderline status in classification.

modelAnswer: Viruses are acellular and show both living and nonliving characteristics.
Therefore, they are not placed in any of the five kingdoms.
